context: Sipho wants to invest a lump sum today at a fixed compound interest rate (a whole-number percentage per annum) so that it grows to a target amount in rand after 2 years. Only the rate and the target amount change between instances; the target is always chosen so that the amount to invest is a whole number of rand, so no rounding is needed.

params.why: the target amount must be a whole number of rand, so that the principal comes out exact

stem: Sipho wants to invest some money at a compound interest rate of ${=r}$ % p.a. How much money should he invest if he wants to reach a sum of $\text{R{=amt}}$ in ${=n}$ years' time?
solution: Read the question carefully and write down the given information: $\begin{aligned}A&=\text{R{=amt}}\\P&=?\\i&=\frac{{=r}}{100}={=fixed(r / 100, 2)}\\n&={=n}\end{aligned}$
To find the amount he must invest, make $P$ the subject of the formula: $\begin{aligned}A&=P(1+i)^{n}\\\frac{A}{(1+i)^{n}}&=P\end{aligned}$
notes: Entry point of the skill: n = 2 only, whole-number rate, and the target is built backwards from a round principal (a multiple of lcm(base, 500) where base = 100^n / gcd(100^n, (100+r)^n)), so A is a whole number and the principal is an exact whole number of rand. This removes the book's 'round up' step on purpose (the book's own questions round up, e.g. 24001.46 -> 24002), which is what the standard and advanced work covers. Exact arithmetic means the key cannot differ by calculator rounding. Example: r = 4, principal 2500 -> A = 2704 (2704 / 1.0816 = 2500). Likely student errors (not used as distractors, since the item is numeric): multiplying A by (1+i)^n instead of dividing, dividing by 1+i once instead of (1+i)^n, or dividing by 1 + n*i (simple-interest habit).
